demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

vignette:
He is 62, a potter who has spent most of his adult life shaping clay with steady hands and a patient eye. Before his loss, his days follow a rhythm he trusts: coffee before dawn, the short walk to the studio behind the house, the wheel turning under his palms while his wife moves in and out of the kitchen garden nearby. They have been married for decades, and their life feels ordinary in a way he values. He thinks of it now as a kind of innocence.

The day she dies begins without warning. She leaves to run a quick errand in town and does not come back. There is a knock on the studio door while he is trimming the foot of a bowl. He remembers the way the clay keeps spinning for a second after he lifts his hands away, and then the sight of two officers standing awkwardly at the threshold. Even now, when he tells it, he can only hold on to fragments: one officer asking if he is her husband, the word “collision,” the phrase “didn’t survive,” his own voice saying “No, that’s not right.” He recalls staring at the wet bowl collapsing inward because no one stops the wheel.

In the first weeks after her death, he moves through arrangements and visitors as if underwater. He sleeps in bursts on the couch with the television on low because the bed feels impossible. At night he hears tires on the road and his body goes rigid before his mind catches up. He startles at knocks on the door. He avoids driving past the intersection where the crash happened, taking a longer route to buy glaze and clay even when it adds half an hour. If someone mentions a car accident on the news, he leaves the room.

The studio, once the place where he feels most himself, becomes unpredictable. At times he works for ten hours straight, forcing out mugs and bowls in a kind of grim endurance, his shoulders locked and jaw tight. At other times he cannot cross the threshold. The smell of wet earth and kiln dust reminds him of that morning because he had been in the middle of making a set of serving dishes they had planned to use for a family dinner. For months, those unfinished pieces sit under plastic, leather-hard and abandoned. When he does throw clay, his mind slips back without consent: the officer at the door, the bowl collapsing, the feeling that the world has tipped out of alignment. He loses whole stretches of time to these memories and then feels ashamed when he notices a wall gone crooked under his hands.

His wife appears everywhere in the house and nowhere he can reach. He keeps her coat on the hook by the door and her gardening gloves on the windowsill, unable to move them, yet he avoids opening the closet because the smell of her soap hits him so hard he cannot breathe. He tells himself he should be grateful for the years they had, but what comes more easily is guilt. He thinks he should have insisted she stay home that day. He replays their last conversation for signs he missed, as if there were some version he could revise that would bring her back. When friends ask how he is doing, he says, “Getting by,” because the real answer feels too large and too strange.

His world gets smaller. He stops going to craft fairs because crowds drain him and he cannot bear the cheerful questions from customers who remember meeting his wife at the register. He no longer teaches weekend pottery classes; the ordinary clatter of students’ voices makes him irritable, and he hates the person he becomes when he snaps at them for small mistakes. His wife used to handle most of the business side of the studio, and now unpaid invoices pile up beside the kiln. He sits with them in his lap, staring, unable to begin.

At night he rarely sleeps more than a few hours. He wakes with his heart pounding from dreams in which he is searching for her in a line of stopped cars, or in which she is calling from somewhere just beyond a closed door. In the morning he feels heavy and dulled, but also on edge, as though something else terrible is waiting. His wife’s death has taught him that catastrophe arrives in the middle of an ordinary day.

He still works, though more slowly. Sometimes he finds himself making narrower forms, vessels with tight openings and thick walls. He notices this but does not comment on it. On better days, the wheel gives him a few minutes of quiet concentration, and he can feel the clay responding to pressure, centering under his hands. Then a truck backfires on the road, or the phone rings unexpectedly, and his whole body jerks before he can stop it.

He loves his wife in the present tense. That is part of what feels confusing to him. People around him speak of moving on, of time doing its work, but he experiences time as split into before and after. He can function, answer questions, load the kiln, speak kindly to neighbors, yet much of him remains fixed at the studio door on the day the officers came, listening to words that still do not feel survivable.
